source.author: lucr
source.text: nam si, ut ipsa petit maiestas cognita rerum, dicendum est, deus ille fuit, deus, inclyte Memmi, qui princeps vitae rationem invenit eam quae nunc appellatur sapientia, quique per artem fluctibus et tantis vitam tantisque tenebris in tam tranquillo et tam clara luce locavit.
source.text_original: nam si, ut ipsa petit maiestas cognita rerum, / dicendum est, deus ille fuit, deus, inclyte Memmi, / qui princeps vitae rationem invenit eam quae / nunc appellatur sapientia, quique per artem / fluctibus et tantis vitam tantisque tenebris / in tam tranquillo et tam clara luce locavit.
source.text_english: For if, as the majesty of the subject itself demands, it must be said, that man was a god, yes, a god, noble Memmius, who first discovered that plan of life which is now called wisdom, and who by his art placed life amid such great storms and such deep darkness in so calm and so bright a light.

reuse.author: lact
reuse.text: nam si, ut ipsa petit maiestas cognita rerum, - dicendum est, deus ille fuit, deus, inclute Memmi tamen non erat sic laudandus deus, quod sapientiam inuenerit, sed quod hominem fecerit qui posset capere sapientiam: minuit enim laudem qui partem laudat ex toto.
reuse.text_original: nam si, ut ipsa petit maiestas cognita rerum, - dicendum est, deus ille fuit, deus, inclute Memmi — tamen non erat sic laudandus deus, quod sapientiam inuenerit, sed quod hominem fecerit qui posset capere sapientiam: minuit enim laudem qui partem laudat ex toto.
reuse.text_english: For if, as the majesty of the thing itself demands—one must say it—that man was a god, a god, illustrious Memmius, yet he would not be worthy of such praise for having discovered wisdom, but for having made the man who could grasp wisdom; for he diminishes praise who praises a part instead of the whole.
